tips.turf-0: In a fast-paced race, front-runners are at a big disadvantage. For front-runners and stalkers, the key is whether they can get away cleanly without being pressed.
tips.turf-1: Few surprises in how the race unfolds; true ability shows. Distance: at 2000m, stalkers drawn wide are at a big disadvantage. Watch out for unfancied horses with a good record.
tips.turf-2: Many races start in front of the stands, so horses that get worked up tend to pull hard. Horses that can sit fairly close to the pace have the edge over deep closers.
tips.dirt-0: The dirt here is easy to pull out of and the straight is long, so closers win surprisingly often. Closers beaten at Nakayama often improve dramatically here. On a heavy track, front-runners dominate.
tips.dirt-1: There aren't many races at this distance. Because it's long, winning from the front is very hard and closers get stronger. Unfancied deep closers ridden without pressure often cause upsets.

tips.turf-0: The straight is short, but deep closers win surprisingly often. If several front-runners look set to push the pace, watch out for closers even when they're unfancied.
tips.turf-1: The pace rarely picks up, so horses without the speed to sit handily struggle. Leading all the way is also hard; target horses that settle well.
tips.turf-2: The race is usually run at a relaxed pace and gets busy from around the third corner. Few surprises: distance suitability and ability show clearly on this course.
tips.dirt-0: In 3-year-old races stalkers rule; without early speed a horse has no chance. For older horses too, early speed is essential. At this distance only, a wide draw is a slight plus.
tips.dirt-1: Even an unfancied front-runner is well worth backing if it's the only one in the race. Early speed matters even more than in sprints, but closers that sneak up the inside often run on for 2nd at long odds.
tips.dirt-2: Races at this distance are very rare. Leading all the way is tough, but a horse has to keep up with the leaders. Focus on stalkers rather than pure front-runners.

tips.turf-0: A fast pace makes life hard for front-runners. Given enough ability, closers win easily on this course whatever the pace.
tips.turf-1: Riders are wary of the hill mid-race, so the pace tends to be fairly steady. Even an unfancied horse that gets an easy lead often hangs on to win.
tips.turf-2: Horses that make their move early on the third-corner hill often tire in the straight. Whatever the pace, favorites tend to run to their ability on this course.
tips.dirt-0: Even at a fairly fast pace, front-runners and stalkers have the edge. Favorites that tend to start slowly or get left behind often run poorly, so be careful.
tips.dirt-1: Going too fast from the start fails, and so does relying purely on a late run. Horses that save energy and kick from the back straight often win on sheer power.

tips.turf-0: The course demands power as well as speed. Horses that lose a duel for the lead tire badly. Quite often the race goes to a front-runner and a deep closer.
tips.turf-1: The usual pattern is a horse leading at the fourth corner and holding on. Another feature is that times are much slower than at other tracks.
tips.turf-2: Front-runners and stalkers have the edge whatever the pace. Even a capable closer struggles unless it's fairly close to the front at the fourth corner.
tips.dirt-0: Even at a fast pace, if the leaders get away cleanly the race is decided among them. If it turns into a scramble, though, unfancied closers come into it.
tips.dirt-1: The track takes stamina, so horses with nothing but speed struggle. A horse that can sit reasonably close without a sharp kick can power home on this course.

tips.turf-0: The turf takes stamina, so speed alone won't win. Front-runners have the edge, but closers often come into it as rivals; half-hearted stalkers actually have it harder.
tips.turf-1: A front-runner that leads alone can survive, but if pressed, the closers sitting just behind pour through. Reading how the race will unfold is the key at this distance.
tips.turf-2: The top-rated horse often wins. Upsets are rare; spread bets from the obvious favorite. Even in lower classes, watch out for stalkers.
tips.dirt-0: It becomes a battle over the front-runner. Stalkers sitting close often tire, so front-runner/closer bets are good value. Front-runner 1-2 finishes are not that common.
tips.dirt-1: In maiden and ¥5M-class races back stalkers; in higher-class races, horses with a proven record are the effective pick. Rather than a front-runner/stalker combo, it's more fun to back a closer with power.

tips.turf-0: Deep closers almost never get there on this course; a horse that takes the lead usually holds on. Only when the track turns bad do closers come into it.
tips.turf-1: On a good track closers can do well too, but late in the meeting, once the track deteriorates, stalkers rule. Check the day's track condition before betting.
tips.turf-2: Basically the race usually suits closers and stalkers can't hold on, but on a heavy track it often becomes a front-runner 1-2.
tips.dirt-0: Front-runners have a high win rate and horses that can't go forward have no chance at all. Judging each horse's early speed is the shortest route to a correct pick.
tips.dirt-1: Even if a horse can't keep up early, it must sweep around from the third corner and join the leading group, or it won't get up. Heavy dirt, so power comes first.

tips.turf-0: On this course you must be up front. Coming from far back only works if the leaders collapse. Target stalkers or horses that can chase the leaders.
tips.turf-1: Even if the pace looks like picking up, stalkers keep their edge. A horse that can lead alone often hangs on even when unfancied.
tips.turf-2: Only 2600m races are run here. The pace is gentle; the usual winner sits 2nd-3rd behind the leader and breaks clear in the straight.
tips.dirt-0: Early speed is a must; horses have to push forward even if it costs them. Back horses ridden by bold, attacking jockeys. Upsets are rare.
tips.dirt-1: Closing is hard on this dirt, so top-2 finishers usually sit handily and hang on. Even at a fast pace the whole field tires and the leaders survive.

tips.turf-0: On the outer circuit the course has a long straight, but it's flat, so stalkers don't stop. However, in big-field higher-class races where the pace rises, closers are the ones to back instead.
tips.turf-1: Stalkers are strongest at this distance. Horses within the first five at the third corner, front-runners included, have the best win rate. On the inner circuit stalkers are even more favored.
tips.dirt-0: At 1000m you must be up front, but 1200m is a distance where closers run on surprisingly well. Versatile horses that can sit just behind the pace probably have the best chance.
tips.dirt-1: Whatever the running style, the first requirement is fitting smoothly into the flow of the race. Unfancied stalkers are dangerous; ignore them and you'll often get burned.

tips.turf-0: The pace is often fast, and for such a tight course closers get there fairly often. Races often end with the two extremes: a front-runner and a deep closer.
tips.turf-1: It becomes a fight between the leader and the closers. The pace isn't very fast, so the key is to narrow it down from the front-runners and stalkers to the closers.
tips.turf-2: Almost always an average-to-slow pace, which favors horses sitting just behind the leader rather than the leader. Upsets are rare at this distance, so bet safely.
tips.dirt-0: Early speed is so important that most winners are in the first three at the fourth corner. Leaders often keep going, so pick horses that can reliably sit up front.
tips.dirt-1: Closers run on reasonably well, but stalkers still rule. Value lies in bets from a popular stalker to horses likely to push forward at all costs.
tips.dirt-2: In any class, a horse that gets an easy lead hangs on unexpectedly well. Such horses are often the ones causing upsets, so always include them as cover.

tips.turf-0: Leading isn't essential, but a horse needs the early speed to sit 2nd-3rd. The danger is an unfancied front-runner: unmarked horses often lead all the way.
tips.turf-1: Even though it's a local track with a short straight, closers often cause upsets at this distance; races are easily close. Look for horses that like flat courses.
tips.turf-2: The pace tends to settle at this distance, so keep in mind that stalkers have the edge in long races. The trend is clearer in ¥5M-class races than in higher-class races.
tips.dirt-0: A horse has to go forward no matter what; without the drive to take the lead it won't work. A horse with speed can cause an upset even when out of form.
tips.dirt-1: Closing from far back is hard; horses must be with the leading group by the fourth corner. Even horses ridden a bit aggressively hang on surprisingly well.

races.name: Oka Sho (Japanese 1000 Guineas)
races.tip: Ignore horses that couldn't win their debut. Last-race form carries straight over, so don't expect out-of-form horses to turn it around. Closers sitting handily are strong.

races.name: Satsuki Sho (Japanese 2000 Guineas)
races.tip: Horses that ran well in prep races over the same distance, like the Yayoi Sho or Wakaba Stakes, are strong. Horses with a sudden burst of speed often explode from behind, more than the power types.

races.name: Tenno Sho (Spring)
races.tip: If three or more G1 winners run, an upset is unlikely. Stayers sometimes charge into 2nd, so checking pedigree is essential.

races.name: Yasuda Kinen
races.tip: This race is run at a fast pace, so many deep closers come charging. A winner of the Keio Hai Spring Cup on good ground has a good chance of finishing top 2.

races.name: Yushun Himba (Japanese Oaks)
races.tip: Since the Oka Sho moved to Hanshin, the link between the races has grown. Focus on horses coming straight from a high Oka Sho finish; avoid bets made only of improving horses.

races.name: Tokyo Yushun (Japanese Derby)
races.tip: Distance suitability backed by pedigree is a must. Horses whose breeding doubts 2400m won't make the top 2 in the Derby. Rate Satsuki Sho runners above the trial-race runners.

races.name: Takarazuka Kinen
races.tip: A race where the top vote-getters in the fan ballot are strong. The Tenno Sho runners clash with the Yasuda Kinen runners; if neither race's winner is running, an upset is possible.

races.name: Tenno Sho (Autumn)
races.tip: A fast pace favors closers, an average pace favors stalkers; it all depends on the pace. A stalker drawn wide is at a disadvantage for that alone.

races.name: Kikuka Sho (Japanese St Leger)
races.tip: However strong a horse is, it struggles unless its pedigree can handle the distance. A stayer pedigree needs watching even when unfancied. For autumn improvers, prep-race form is what counts.

races.name: Queen Elizabeth II Cup
races.tip: Back horses improving in autumn over horses that shone in spring. Horses arriving on a winning streak deserve extra attention. Horses bred for longer distances than the Oaks often come into it.

races.name: Mile Championship
races.tip: Deep closers look like getting there but don't. Early speed is a must. Horses coming from the autumn Tenno Sho have a better record than Swan Stakes runners.

races.name: Japan Cup
races.tip: In-form horses from Oceania and America run better than horses with European records. A horse that won a graded race of 2400m+ in its last three starts can't be ignored, even when unfancied.

races.name: Hanshin 3yo Stakes
races.tip: As a race for 3-year-old fillies, over-trusting the favorites is a mistake. Hanshin's track is heavy, so horses can compete without good times on record. Beware a big run from a deep closer.

races.name: Asahi Hai 3yo Stakes
races.tip: Winning with one late run down the straight is nearly impossible; without early speed a horse can't compete. Few upsets: horses that have run strong races usually power home.

races.name: Sprinters Stakes
races.tip: Speed alone won't win. The pace is often furiously fast, and closers that saved energy until the straight run on. Fillies and colts are evenly matched.

races.name: Arima Kinen
races.tip: With 3-year-olds and older horses mixed, a messy race can bring a huge upset. The top finisher from the Kikuka Sho can be trusted; the top finisher from the Japan Cup is risky.
